newsitem.title: USA: Alaska fishermen sue for better spill protection.
newsitem.headline: Alaska fishermen sue for better spill protection.

text.p: Alaska's commercial fishermen, dissatisfied with spill-contingeny plans approved by the state more than a year ago, have filed a lawsuit seeking tighter safety rules for oil shipping.
In the lawsuit, filed in state Superior Court on Thursday, fishing groups said the plans were inadequate to protect areas harmed by the 1989 Exxon Valdez disaster from another major oil spill.

The Alaska Department of Environmental Conservation (DEC) failed to meet all the requirements of state law when it reviewed spill-contingency plans submitted by the 21 companies that ship oil through Prince William Sound, the lawsuit said.

"The facts of the process tell a tale of unnecessary delay, expense and hardship to the very parties who suffered most from the tragedy of the Exxon Valdez -- and who stand to suffer again when the next spill occurs," said the lawsuit, filed by Cordova District Fishermen United, United Fishermen of Alaska and two individuals against DEC.

The DEC approved the plans in August 1995, despite objections from fishermen in Kodiak and Cordova who said their regions -- on the edge of the Trans Alaska Pipeline System shipping routes -- were left exposed to risks.
Appeals by the fishing groups went unheeded, said Cheri Shaw, executive director of Cordova District Fishermen United.

"It's been 14 months with nothing. We're just concerned about having oil transported through Prince William Sound and outside Prince William Sound without an adequate contingency plan," she said Friday.

Memories of the 11 million gallon (41.6 million litre) Exxon Valdez oil spill were still fresh for the fishermen, Shaw said. "We live in a beautiful state with plenty of marine life and bird life. We don't want to see anything happen to it," she said.
In addition, the fishermen want better fire-safety rules for oil tankers, better technology for tugs that escort laden tankers and more cleanup equipment mandated for large spills, Shaw said.
According to a law passed by the state legislature in 1990, oil shippers in Prince William Sound must be able to respond to and contain an Exxon Valdez-sized spill within 72 hours.
DEC officials were not immediately available for comment on Friday.
